text:
So picking a model comes down to what you're counting. One yes or no is Bernoulli. Successes in a fixed number of tries, binomial. Tries until the first success, geometric. Events at a steady rate, with no fixed number, Poisson. All four count in whole numbers. If two point seven makes sense, you're measuring, not counting.

Measurements work differently. Take waiting times, which are often exponential: short waits are common, and long ones rare. Say they average five minutes. What's the chance a wait is EXACTLY five? Not five and a bit. Exactly five... and the answer is zero. A single point has no width, so it holds no probability. Probability lives on ranges, as area under the curve. Waits between two and eight minutes take up forty-seven percent of it. In code, that's the area left of eight, minus the area left of two. Which means the curve's height can't be a probability.

Spread a value evenly from zero to ten, and its curve is flat, a uniform, at a height of point one. Three to seven covers four tenths of the width, so it holds four tenths of the probability. Now squeeze all of it into half a unit. To keep the area at one, the height has to climb to two. Two isn't a two hundred percent chance. It's a density, probability per unit of width. Only the area has to come to one. Often, though, you need the question the other way round.

Say response times average two hundred milliseconds, and you want the time that ninety-five percent of requests beat. Plot the share finished by each moment. Go across from ninety-five percent, then down... five hundred and ninety-nine milliseconds. That's a quantile, the area read backwards. It's how you set a cutoff, or a promise to customers. And of all these shapes, one turns up more than any other.
